fetched_contents.text: Nrf2 and Oxidative Stress: A General Overview of Mechanisms and Implications in Human Disease Abstract Organisms are continually exposed to exogenous and endogenous sources of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and other oxidants that have both beneficial and deleterious effects on the cell. ROS have important roles in a wide range of physiological processes; however, high ROS levels are associated with oxidative stress and disease progression. Oxidative stress has been implicated in nearly all major human diseases, from neurogenerative diseases and neuropsychiatric disorders to cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and cancer. Antioxidant defence systems have evolved as a means of protection against oxidative stress, with the transcription factor Nrf2 as the key regulator. Nrf2 is responsible for regulating an extensive panel of antioxidant enzymes involved in the detoxification and elimination of oxidative stress and has been extensively studied in the disease contexts. This review aims to provide the reader with a general overview of oxidative stress and Nrf2, including basic mechanisms of Nrf2 activation and regulation, and implications in various major human diseases. Keywords: Nrf2, oxidative stress, antioxidant, antioxidant response 1. Oxidative Stress 1.1. Reactive Oxygen Species Free radicals are unstable atoms, ions, or molecules containing one or more unpaired electrons in the outermost electron shell. An unpaired valence electron is unstable and highly reactive. To attain stability, free radicals attack and acquire electrons from other compounds or molecules within their proximity. The attacked entity loses an electron to become oxidized and becomes a free radical itself, thereby initiating a chain reaction that can result in cellular damage [1]. ROS and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) are unstable molecules containing oxygen and/or nitrogen and include both free radical and non-radical species. The oxygen molecule (O2••) is a weak free radical itself due to the presence of two unpaired electrons in its valence shell; however, it is less reactive than other oxygen species due to the parallel spin of its electrons [2]. Major ROS and RNS are listed in Table 1. Table 1. Major Reactive Oxygen and Reactive Nitrogen Species. They are produced when nitric oxide (•NO) reacts with oxygen species. For example, nitric oxide can react with superoxide (O2•−) to form peroxynitrite (ONOO−): •NO + O2•−→ONOO− (1) Peroxynitrite is very reactive and readily attacks lipid molecules, resulting in lipid peroxidation and lipoprotein oxidation [3]. However, like ROS, low levels of RNS have important roles in physiological processes. For example, nitric oxide produced by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) regulates blood vessel dilation and is involved in synaptic transmission in the brain [4,5]. On the other hand, high levels of RNS result in nitrosative stress, macromolecule damage, and activation of transcription factors NF-ΚB and activator protein 1 (AP-1) involved in inflammation and other pathological pathways [6,7]. RNS and ROS often act together to cause cellular damage [8]. ROS are oxidants (i.e., a molecule that removes electrons from other molecules) predominantly produced as byproducts of cellular metabolism and biochemical processes within the cell. Mitochondria are a primary source of ROS produced by aerobic respiration [9,10,11,12], where the reduction of molecular oxygen in the electron transport chain results in the leaking of superoxide radicals which are readily detoxified to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) by antioxidant enzymes such as catalase and glutathione peroxidase. Hydrogen peroxide may react with transition metals such as iron (Fe2+) to produce hydroxyl radicals via the Fenton reaction to further produce hydroxyl radicals (•OH) which are highly reactive toward all components of DNA molecules as well as lipids [13]. Peroxisomes also generate ROS from aerobic metabolism [14], and phagocytic neutrophils and macrophages produce ROS to eliminate invading pathogens [15]. At low to moderate levels, ROS plays an important role in normal cellular processes, serving as secondary messengers in intracellular signalling cascades that mediate cell growth, autophagy, inflammatory and immune function, and contribute to overall redox regulation [16,17]. However, both radical and non-radical ROS can be powerful oxidants that are detrimental to the cell upon high or chronic exposure. Toxic exogenous sources of ROS include pollution, tobacco smoke, alcohol, ozone, environmental and industrial toxins, and radiation [1]. Due to their reactive nature, ROS production and elimination must be strictly regulated by the cell. In this scenario, there is an imbalance between the production of ROS and cellular defence mechanisms against oxidative stress, i.e., the antioxidant response. Chronic oxidative stress and the resultant oxidative damage have been implicated in many human diseases including cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, cancer, and the aging process [18,19,20,21,22]. fetched_contents.text: Metabolic Dysfunction‐Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD): Mechanisms, Clinical Implications and Therapeutic Advances ABSTRACT Introduction Metabolic Dysfunction‐Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) has emerged as the most prevalent chronic liver disease worldwide, affecting ~25%–30% of the adult population, with higher prevalence observed in individuals with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Among reported MASLD cases, prevalence is consistently higher in men than in women, and global incidence has risen by ~50% over the past two decades, mirroring the global rise in obesity and metabolic syndrome. MASLD encompasses a spectrum of hepatic pathologies ranging from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, fibrosis and cirrhosis. Despite its high prevalence, the heterogeneity in disease progression and relative absence of approved pharmacological therapies pose challenges for effective clinical management. Methods and Results This review synthesises current literature on MASLD across epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation and treatment. Key molecular mechanisms, including lipid metabolism dysregulation, insulin resistance and mitochondrial dysfunction, are examined with a focus on understanding the basis for progression to metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatohepatitis (MASH). Clinical manifestations, diagnostic tools and risk stratification systems for MASLD are summarised. Current and emerging therapies such as lifestyle interventions, pharmacological agents and microbiome‐targeted strategies are reviewed. The review also highlights ongoing challenges, including diagnostic limitations, disease heterogeneity and disparities in care. Conclusion MASLD is a complex, multifactorial liver disease with a growing public health impact, driven by the rising prevalence of metabolic syndrome. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a critical nexus linking genetic susceptibility to metabolic stress and inflammatory responses. Preclinical models that capture these mitochondrial contributions are vital for therapeutic discovery and for advancing personalised medicine approaches in MASLD care. Keywords: mitochondrial dysfunction‐associated steatohepatitis (MASH), mitochondrial dysfunction‐associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), mitochondrial genetics, Western‐style diet ---------------------------------------- Healthy liver function depends on the coordinated activity of hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, stellate cells, endothelial cells and cholangiocytes. During MASLD, all cell types undergo pathological changes, driving steatosis, inflammation, fibrosis, impaired exchange and ductular reactions. This work highlights how diverse liver cells cooperatively fuel disease progression and compromise organ function. 1. Introduction A critical factor in metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) pathophysiology is mitochondrial dysfunction, or mitochondriopathy, which impairs lipid metabolism leading to lipid accumulation, and increases in oxidative stress, reducing energy production [1]. These processes occur within the highly specialised microenvironment of the liver, a multifunctional organ responsible for regulating systemic energy metabolism, detoxification, immune surveillance and synthesis of essential proteins and bile acids [2]. Central to this role is the liver's regulation of glucose homeostasis, achieved through glycogen storage and mobilisation, gluconeogenesis and integration of fatty acid metabolism, positioning it as a key determinant of whole‐body energy balance [3]. The interplay between diverse cell types within the liver is critical in the progression from simple steatosis to inflammation and fibrosis (Figure 1). Hepatocytes, the primary parenchymal cells, constitute approximately 70%–80% of the liver's mass and play a central role in lipid and glucose homeostasis [4]. Non‐parenchymal cells, including Kupffer cells (resident macrophages), hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) and cholangiocytes, support immune regulation, fibrogenesis, vascular integrity and bile secretion, respectively [5, 6]. MASLD, formerly known as non‐alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), represents a spectrum of liver pathologies characterised by excessive fat accumulation in hepatocytes in the absence of significant alcohol consumption, and is associated with metabolic syndrome (defined as the presence of at least three of: elevated waist circumference, impaired fasting glucose, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia or low HDL cholesterol) [7] (Figure 2). The recent shift in nomenclature from NAFLD to MASLD reflects a more accurate framing of the condition as a metabolic disorder, centering diagnostic criteria on metabolic dysfunction rather than exclusion of alcohol use [8]. This reclassification aims to improve diagnostic clarity and align with emerging evidence linking liver disease to systemic metabolic derangements. A subset of MASLD patients develops metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatohepatitis (MASH), formerly known as non‐alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), a more severe form of the disease marked by hepatic inflammation and fibrosis, which significantly increases the risk of progression to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [9]. Both genetic and metabolic factors impact MASLD progression and severity. For example, cardiometabolic diseases, which comprise a constellation of obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia and hypertension, are well‐established drivers of MASLD progression [10, 11]. Insulin resistance promotes hepatic lipogenesis (excessive fatty acid synthesis) and impairs lipid clearance, while dyslipidemia exacerbates hepatic fat deposition [12, 13]. Systemic hypertension also further contributes to disease progression through vascular inflammatory mechanisms [14]. 1.1. fetched_contents.text: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease-induced changes in the antioxidant system: a review Abstract Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a heterogeneous condition characterized by liver steatosis, inflammation, consequent fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Chronic impairment of lipid metabolism is closely related to oxidative stress, leading to cellular lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endoplasmic reticulum stress. The detrimental effect of oxidative stress is usually accompanied by changes in antioxidant defense mechanisms, with the alterations in antioxidant enzymes expression/activities during MASLD development and progression reported in many clinical and experimental studies. This review will provide a comprehensive overview of the present research on MASLD-induced changes in the catalytic activity and expression of the main antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutases, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, glutathione S-transferases, glutathione reductase, NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase) and in the level of non-enzymatic antioxidant glutathione. Furthermore, an overview of the therapeutic effects of vitamin E on antioxidant enzymes during the progression of MASLD will be presented. Generally, at the beginning of MASLD development, the expression/activity of antioxidant enzymes usually increases to protect organisms against the increased production of reactive oxygen species. However, in advanced stage of MASLD, the expression/activity of several antioxidants generally decreases due to damage to hepatic and extrahepatic cells, which further exacerbates the damage. Although the results obtained in patients, in various experimental animal or cell models have been inconsistent, taken together the importance of antioxidant enzymes in MASLD development and progression has been clearly shown. Keywords: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, Antioxidant enzyme, Glutathione, Expression, Catalytic activity Introduction Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), previously referred to as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, is the most common liver disease, afflicting about 25–30% of the general population worldwide. Occurring in individuals who drink little to no alcohol, MASLD is characterized by hepatic fat accumulation (Korinkova et al. 2020; Perumpail et al. 2017; Rinella et al. 2023). This heterogenous and complex disease encompasses a broad clinical spectrum of liver abnormalities which vary in the severity of the injury and the resulting fibrosis. At one end of the spectrum, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver (hepatic steatosis, MASL) may progress to a more advanced state called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) characterized by significant hepatocyte damage, inflammation, and pericellular fibrosis, and further to cirrhosis (Friedman et al. 2018; Rinella et al. 2023). The pathogenesis of MASLD is complex, multifactorial, and not yet fully understood. Therefore, identification of the molecular mechanisms leading to MASLD-related fat accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress is necessary to facilitate the development of specific interventions aimed at preventing the progression of hepatic steatosis. As no pharmacotherapy for MASLD has been approved at present, lifestyle changes represent the mainstay of therapy. Although lifestyle interventions have proven to be effective in MASLD management, achieving and sustaining such changes may be difficult for many patients (e.g. Finer 2022; Hannah and Harrison 2016)). In this review, we summarize the pathogenesis of MASLD with an emphasis on oxidative stress and MASLD-induced changes in antioxidant pathways. A brief introduction to the pathogenesis of MASLD Based on the histological findings, MASLD is categorized as MASL and MASH. MASL is characterized by mixed macrovesicular and microvesicular hepatic steatosis (≥ 5% hepatocytes) which may be accompanied by mild inflammation, with the risk of progression to cirrhosis and liver failure considered minimal. In 10–20% of patients, hepatic steatosis progresses to a more advanced state called MASH, which is characterized by the presence of hepatic steatosis (≥ 5% hepatocytes), inflammation, and hepatocyte injury (ballooning) with or without fibrosis. MASH can progress to cirrhosis, liver failure, and even to hepatocellular carcinoma in rare cases (Fig. 1). Cirrhosis is the most frequent reason for a liver transplant (Hardy et al. 2016; Chalasani et al. 2018). Pathogenesis of MASLD is closely related to metabolic syndrome. In patients with MASLD, features of metabolic syndrome (such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia) are highly prevalent and increase the risk of MASLD development (Chalasani et al. 2018). According to the currently accepted multiple-hit theory, several simultaneously acting “hits” (e.g. insulin resistance, excessive secretion of adipokines, unhealthy lifestyle, gut dysmicrobiosis) act together on a genetically predisposed person to induce MASLD (Buzzetti et al. 2016). According to this theory, oxidative stress plays an important role in MASLD progression as the starting point of hepatic damage (Masarone et al. 2018). In following subsection, the effect of hepatic oxidative stress on the pathogenesis of MASLD will be discussed. Genetic and epigenetic factors determining MASLD have been recently reviewed by Jonas and Schurmann (Jonas and Schurmann 2021), and the role of gut microbiota in mediating MASLD development was summarized by Campo et al. (Campo et al. 2019). Clinical and histopathological consequences of oxidative stress in MASLD

Oxidative stress is a central driver of MASLD progression and severity, with the evidence here pointing to a clear sequence from steatosis to inflammation, fibrosis, and beyond. The MASLD review states that MASLD is a spectrum of liver pathologies ranging from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, and that mitochondrial dysfunction impairs lipid metabolism and increases oxidative stress, reducing energy production [N2-F2]. Another MASLD review specifically links oxidative stress to lipid metabolism dysregulation, insulin resistance, and mitochondrial dysfunction, emphasizing that oxidative stress is part of the pathogenesis of MASLD and contributes to disease progression [N2-R1]. The same evidence also notes that oxidative stress can augment de novo lipid levels and increase lipid accumulation, creating a “vicious cycle” in MAFLD [N2-R3]. This supports the idea that oxidative stress is not merely a downstream consequence of steatosis but actively reinforces it.

In terms of histopathology, oxidative stress contributes to inflammation and fibrosis. The oxidative stress in liver disease review explicitly states that oxidative stress plays a crucial role in liver disease progression to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [N3-R1]. Another MASLD review states that oxidative/nitrosative stress is caused by imbalance between ROS/RNS and antioxidant defenses, and that this imbalance leads to cellular lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endoplasmic reticulum stress [N5-F3]. The review also notes that oxidative stress is accompanied by changes in antioxidant defense mechanisms, and that in advanced MASLD, antioxidant enzyme expression/activity generally decreases, exacerbating damage [N5-F3]. This mechanism helps explain why oxidative stress drives inflammation and fibrosis: it disrupts redox balance, injures hepatocytes, and promotes the recruitment of inflammatory cells and fibrogenic responses [N2-F2][N5-F3].

The evidence also supports a strong association between oxidative stress and disease progression or severity. The MASLD review explicitly states that oxidative stress is a starting point of hepatic damage and is important in MASLD progression [N5-F3]. The same review also notes that MASLD is heterogeneous and complex, with progression from MASL to MASH to cirrhosis, and that oxidative stress is part of the pathogenic process leading to this spectrum [N5-F3]. The oxidative stress in liver disease review similarly states that oxidative stress not only contributes to the development of NAFLD but also regulates inflammatory pathways, particularly those involved in disease progression [N3-R2]. Taken together, these sources indicate that higher oxidative stress is associated with more severe disease, more inflammation, and more fibrosis [N2-F2][N3-R2][N5-F3].

Evidence for cirrhosis or advanced fibrosis linked to ROS/RNS elevation is explicit. The MASLD review notes that MASLD encompasses a spectrum from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis [N2-F2]. It also states that oxidative stress is closely linked to the progression of MAFLD, which is consistent with advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis [N2-R3]. The oxidative stress in liver disease review specifically states that oxidative stress plays a crucial role in liver disease progression to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC [N3-R1]. The MASLD review further notes that advanced stage MASLD is associated with decreased antioxidant enzyme activity and that this exacerbates damage [N5-F3]. This suggests that ROS/RNS elevation in MASLD is not only a biomarker of disease activity but also a contributor to advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis [N3-R1][N5-F3].

Beyond liver disease, oxidative stress has cardiovascular and metabolic consequences. The MASLD review notes that oxidative stress is closely linked to cardiovascular complications such as atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure [N2-R5]. The same review also states that oxidative stress and mitochondrial antioxidant defense depletion play an important role in disease progression in MAFLD/NASH [N3-R5]. This indicates that oxidative stress in MASLD extends beyond the liver and is associated with systemic metabolic complications, including hypertension and cardiovascular disease [N2-R5][N3-R5]. The evidence does not explicitly quantify these consequences across all MASLD subgroups, but it clearly establishes a broader metabolic and cardiovascular burden.

Overall, the clinical and histopathological consequences of oxidative stress in MASLD are substantial: it worsens steatosis, promotes inflammation, drives fibrosis and cirrhosis, and is linked to cardiovascular and metabolic complications beyond the liver [N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2][N5-F3][N2-R5].

Mechanistic pathways linking impaired antioxidant activity to ROS/RNS elevation in MASLD

The evidence here identifies several antioxidant enzymes most commonly impaired in liver disease, with glutathione, superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and Nrf2-related pathways emerging as central players. The Nrf2 review states that Nrf2 regulates an extensive panel of antioxidant enzymes involved in detoxification and elimination of oxidative stress [N1-F1]. It also notes that Nrf2 acts as a pivotal part of the ARE-mediated expression of oxidative stress enzyme genes, including antioxidant and detoxicant genes [N1-R2]. The oxidative stress in liver disorders review lists SOD, catalase (CAT), and glutathione peroxidases among the enzymes catalyzing ROS detoxification [N1-R3]. The MASLD review further states that oxidative/nitrosative stress is caused by imbalance between ROS/RNS and antioxidant defenses, and that antioxidant enzyme expression/activity changes during MASLD development and progression [N5-F3]. Taken together, these sources indicate that the most commonly impaired antioxidant systems in liver disease are the Nrf2-regulated antioxidant enzymes, SOD, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, and glutathione-related pathways [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-F3].

Reduced enzyme activity affects ROS/RNS production and clearance in a classic redox imbalance. The Nrf2 review explains that Nrf2 is responsible for regulating antioxidant enzymes involved in detoxification and elimination of oxidative stress, and that its activation is central to the antioxidant response [N1-F1]. The oxidative stress in liver disorders review explains that ROS are produced as byproducts of cellular metabolism and that hydrogen peroxide can be detoxified by catalase and glutathione peroxidase [N1-R3]. The MASLD review notes that oxidative stress is caused by imbalance between ROS/RNS production and antioxidant defenses, and that this imbalance leads to cellular lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endoplasmic reticulum stress [N5-F3]. It also states that in advanced MASLD, antioxidant enzyme expression/activity generally decreases, further exacerbating damage [N5-F3]. This indicates that impaired antioxidant activity increases ROS/RNS burden, while intact enzyme activity helps clear them [N1-F1][N1-R3][N5-F3].

Nrf2, glutathione, SOD, and catalase interact in a coordinated redox defense network. Nrf2 is the master transcription factor that upregulates antioxidant enzymes, including SOD, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, glutathione S-transferases, and glutathione reductase [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Glutathione is described as maintaining a reduced cellular environment and mitigating oxidative damage to proteins [N5-R5]. SOD detoxifies superoxide radicals into hydrogen peroxide, while catalase further breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen [N1-R3]. The MASLD review explicitly links these pathways to oxidative/nitrosative stress and states that antioxidant defense changes accompany oxidative stress [N5-F3]. This means that Nrf2 activation enhances the production of enzymes that clear ROS, while glutathione provides a second-line antioxidant defense and catalase helps convert hydrogen peroxide into less reactive products [N1-F1][N1-R3][N5-F3][N5-R5].

Lipid metabolism and insulin resistance modulate these pathways. The MASLD review states that MASLD is closely related to metabolic syndrome, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia [N2-F2]. It also notes that oxidative stress is the starting point of hepatic damage and is important in MASLD progression [N5-F3]. The oxidative stress in liver disease review states that oxidative stress is closely linked to cardiovascular complications such as atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure [N2-R5]. The MASLD review also notes that lipid metabolism dysregulation, insulin resistance, and mitochondrial dysfunction are key features of MASLD [N2-F2][N5-F3]. This suggests that lipid accumulation and insulin resistance increase ROS/RNS production and reduce antioxidant capacity, thereby worsening redox imbalance [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In turn, redox imbalance can impair lipid metabolism, creating a feedback loop that exacerbates steatosis and inflammation [N2-F2][N5-F3].

In summary, impaired antioxidant activity in MASLD is most clearly reflected in reduced SOD, catalase, and glutathione-related defenses, with Nrf2 as the upstream regulator of these enzymes [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-F3]. Reduced enzyme activity increases ROS/RNS burden, while intact enzyme activity helps clear oxidants [N1-R3][N5-F3]. Nrf2, glutathione, SOD, and catalase work together to defend against ROS/RNS, but lipid metabolism and insulin resistance can disrupt this network, worsening redox imbalance and disease progression [N2-F2][N5-F3][N2-R5].

Evidence gaps and limitations in current MASLD oxidative stress research

Current MASLD oxidative stress research has several important gaps and limitations. First, patient populations and endpoints are under-represented, particularly in the translation of findings from animal models to humans. The MASLD review states that oxidative stress is closely linked to cardiovascular complications such as atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure, but it also notes that results obtained in patients, various experimental animal or cell models have been inconsistent [N5-F3]. Another MASLD oxidative stress study aimed to compare redox profiles between MASLD mice and MASLD patients, but the animal model and human manifestations differed [N6-R2]. This indicates that the evidence base is not evenly distributed across human studies, and that many findings remain model-dependent rather than directly validated in MASLD patients [N6-R2][N5-F3].

Second, biomarkers do not always reflect true oxidative stress well. The oxidative stress in liver disease review states that oxidative stress not only contributes to NAFLD but also regulates inflammatory pathways [N3-R2], which suggests that biomarker elevation may be a downstream or indirect marker rather than a direct readout of oxidative stress itself. The MASLD review also notes that antioxidant enzyme expression/activity changes during MASLD development and progression, but that results across patients, animal models, and cell models have been inconsistent [N5-F3]. This inconsistency implies that current biomarkers may not reliably capture the true redox state in MASLD and may be influenced by disease stage, comorbidities, or measurement methods [N5-F3][N3-R2].

Third, animal or cell-based findings do not always translate directly to humans. The MASLD review explicitly states that results obtained in patients and various experimental models have been inconsistent [N5-F3]. The MASLD oxidative stress study comparing MASLD mice and MASLD patients found differences in redox profiles between the two groups [N6-R2]. This suggests that animal models may not fully recapitulate human disease, especially because oxidative stress and antioxidant defenses are not identical across species or across disease stages [N6-R2][N5-F3]. The review on animal models of MASLD also emphasizes that animal models are used to study the disease, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and needs careful comparison to human disease [N6-R4]. This limitation is especially important for therapeutic development, where preclinical findings may not predict clinical outcomes [N6-R4][N5-F3].

Fourth, redox profile comparisons across models and patients are limited by heterogeneity and inconsistency. The MASLD review states that antioxidant enzyme expression/activity changes during MASLD development and progression, and that results across patients, animal models, and cell models have been inconsistent [N5-F3]. The MASLD oxidative stress study comparing MASLD mice and MASLD patients found that the manifestation of redox profiles differed between the model and the human group [N6-R2]. The review on animal models of MASLD notes that the disease pathogenesis and used animal models were summarized through PubMed, implying that model selection and comparison are not standardized [N6-R4]. These limitations make it difficult to draw consistent conclusions about redox profiles across studies and to identify universal biomarkers or therapeutic targets [N5-F3][N6-R2][N6-R4].

Overall, the evidence gaps in MASLD oxidative stress research are substantial: under-represented human patient populations and endpoints, inconsistent biomarker interpretation, limited translatability from animal and cell models, and heterogeneous redox profile comparisons across models and patients [N5-F3][N6-R2][N6-R4]. These limitations mean that current findings should be interpreted cautiously and that more human studies are needed to validate redox mechanisms and biomarkers in MASLD [N5-F3][N6-R2].

## Integrated clinical consequences of impaired antioxidant activity and elevated ROS/RNS in MASLD

In MASLD, impaired antioxidant enzyme activity and elevated reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS) are not merely bystander phenomena; they are central drivers of disease progression, severity, and broader metabolic complications. The evidence from the three branch reports converges on a single picture: oxidative stress worsens steatosis, promotes inflammation, drives fibrosis and cirrhosis, and extends beyond the liver to cardiovascular and metabolic disease [N2-F2][N3-R1][N5-F3][N2-R5]. At the same time, the mechanistic and translational literature shows that antioxidant defenses such as Nrf2, glutathione, SOD, and catalase are the primary systems affected, while lipid metabolism and insulin resistance amplify redox imbalance [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-F3][N2-F2].

### 1) How impaired antioxidant activity and elevated ROS/RNS contribute to MASLD progression

The core mechanism is a failure of the liver’s antioxidant defense system. Nrf2 is the master regulator of antioxidant enzymes, including SOD, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, glutathione S-transferases, glutathione reductase, and other protective proteins involved in detoxification and elimination of oxidative stress [N1-F1][N1-R2]. When this system is impaired, ROS/RNS production exceeds clearance, leading to oxidative/nitrosative stress. The MASLD review explicitly states that oxidative/nitrosative stress is caused by imbalance between ROS/RNS and antioxidant defenses, and that this imbalance leads to cellular lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endoplasmic reticulum stress [N5-F3]. It also notes that antioxidant enzyme expression/activity changes during MASLD development and progression, with decreased antioxidant capacity in advanced disease [N5-F3].

This means that impaired antioxidant enzyme activity does not simply reduce ROS clearance; it shifts the liver into a pro-oxidant state in which ROS/RNS accumulate, oxidize lipids and proteins, and damage mitochondrial function. The same review states that oxidative stress is closely linked to cardiovascular complications such as atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure, highlighting a broader metabolic burden [N2-R5]. The MASLD review further links oxidative stress to lipid metabolism dysregulation, insulin resistance, and mitochondrial dysfunction, emphasizing that oxidative stress is a starting point of hepatic damage and important in MASLD progression [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In other words, reduced antioxidant capacity worsens the redox environment, which in turn worsens lipid accumulation and insulin resistance, creating a self-reinforcing cycle [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 2) Clinical and histopathological consequences of oxidative stress in MASLD

Oxidative stress is a central driver of MASLD progression and severity. The MASLD review describes MASLD as a spectrum from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, with mitochondrial dysfunction impairing lipid metabolism and increasing oxidative stress [N2-F2]. The oxidative stress in liver disease review states that oxidative stress plays a crucial role in liver disease progression to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [N3-R1]. This supports the idea that oxidative stress is not only a downstream feature of MASLD but an active contributor to disease severity.

At the histopathological level, oxidative stress promotes inflammation and fibrosis. The oxidative stress in liver disease review explicitly states that oxidative stress regulates inflammatory pathways [N3-R2], while the MASLD review notes that oxidative/nitrosative stress leads to cellular lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endoplasmic reticulum stress [N5-F3]. This aligns with the broader pathophysiology of MASLD: oxidative stress injures hepatocytes, recruits inflammatory cells, and activates fibrogenic responses [N2-F2][N3-R1][N5-F3]. The review also notes that in advanced MASLD, antioxidant enzyme expression/activity generally decreases, further exacerbating damage [N5-F3]. That is, ROS/RNS elevation in the early stages may be compensated by upregulated antioxidant defenses, but in later stages, the system fails and disease worsens.

Evidence for cirrhosis or advanced fibrosis linked to ROS/RNS elevation is strong. The MASLD review states that MASLD encompasses a spectrum from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis [N2-F2]. The oxidative stress in liver disease review states that oxidative stress plays a crucial role in liver disease progression to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC [N3-R1]. The MASLD review also notes that oxidative stress is closely linked to cardiovascular complications, including atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure [N2-R5]. Taken together, these sources indicate that ROS/RNS elevation is associated with advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis, as well as with systemic metabolic complications [N3-R1][N2-R5].

### 3) Beyond the liver: cardiovascular and metabolic consequences

The evidence goes well beyond the liver. Oxidative stress in MASLD is closely linked to cardiovascular complications such as atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure [N2-R5]. The MASLD review also states that oxidative stress and mitochondrial antioxidant defense depletion play an important role in disease progression in MAFLD/NASH [N3-R5]. This means that impaired antioxidant activity and elevated ROS/RNS are not confined to hepatic injury; they contribute to broader metabolic dysfunction and cardiovascular disease [N2-R5][N3-R5].

These effects are likely amplified by lipid metabolism and insulin resistance. The MASLD review states that MASLD is closely related to metabolic syndrome, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia [N2-F2]. It also notes that oxidative stress is the starting point of hepatic damage and is important in MASLD progression [N5-F3]. This implies that lipid accumulation and insulin resistance increase ROS/RNS production and reduce antioxidant capacity, creating a feedback loop that worsens redox imbalance [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In turn, redox imbalance can impair lipid metabolism, further fueling steatosis and inflammation [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 4) What the evidence says about biomarkers and translational limits

The evidence base for oxidative stress in MASLD is substantial, but it is not yet definitive. The branch reports emphasize that biomarkers are important but not fully reliable. The oxidative stress in liver disease review states that oxidative stress not only contributes to NAFLD but also regulates inflammatory pathways [N3-R2], suggesting that biomarker elevation may reflect downstream or indirect changes rather than a direct readout of oxidative stress. The MASLD review notes that antioxidant enzyme expression/activity changes during MASLD development and progression, but that results across patients, animal models, and cell models have been inconsistent [N5-F3]. This inconsistency limits how well biomarkers reflect the true redox state in MASLD [N5-F3][N3-R2].

Translational limitations are also clear. The MASLD oxidative stress study comparing MASLD mice and MASLD patients found differences in redox profiles between the two groups, indicating that animal models do not always mirror human disease [N6-R2]. The MASLD review similarly states that results obtained in patients and various experimental models have been inconsistent [N5-F3]. The review on animal models of MASLD emphasizes that animal models are used to study the disease, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and needs careful comparison to human disease [N6-R4]. These limitations mean that preclinical findings may not directly predict clinical outcomes [N6-R2][N6-R4].

### 5) Practical implications for clinical care

In practical terms, the clinical consequences of impaired antioxidant activity and elevated ROS/RNS in MASLD are multiple and interconnected. First, oxidative stress worsens steatosis and drives inflammation and fibrosis, making it a key contributor to disease severity [N2-F2][N3-R1][N5-F3]. Second, it is associated with advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis [N3-R1][N2-R5]. Third, it extends beyond the liver to cardiovascular and metabolic complications [N2-R5][N3-R5]. Fourth, the antioxidant system itself is impaired in MASLD, with Nrf2, SOD, catalase, and glutathione pathways central to redox defense [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R5]. Finally, lipid metabolism and insulin resistance modulate these pathways, creating a vicious cycle in which oxidative stress and metabolic dysfunction reinforce each other [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 6) Bottom line

In patients with MASLD, impaired antioxidant enzyme activity and elevated ROS/RNS levels are major contributors to disease progression and severity. They worsen steatosis, promote inflammation, drive fibrosis and cirrhosis, and are linked to cardiovascular and metabolic complications beyond the liver [N2-F2][N3-R1][N5-F3][N2-R5][N3-R5]. The main antioxidant defenses involved are Nrf2-regulated antioxidant enzymes, SOD, catalase, and glutathione-related pathways, which work together to clear ROS/RNS [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R5]. However, the evidence base has important limitations: biomarkers are not always reliable, animal and cell studies do not always translate to humans, and redox profile comparisons across models and patients are inconsistent [N5-F3][N6-R2][N6-R4]. For clinical care, these findings suggest that antioxidant dysfunction is not just a passive consequence of MASLD, but a clinically meaningful target for intervention and a key reason why oxidative stress remains a central theme in MASLD research [N2-F2][N3-R1][N5-F3][N2-R5].

The MASLD review explicitly states that oxidative stress is a starting point of hepatic damage and is important in MASLD progression [N5-F3]. Taken together, these sources indicate that the most commonly impaired antioxidant systems in liver disease are the Nrf2-regulated antioxidant enzymes, SOD, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, and glutathione-related pathways [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-F3].

Reduced enzyme activity increases ROS/RNS burden, while intact enzyme activity helps clear oxidants [N1-R3][N5-F3]. In MASLD, impaired antioxidant enzyme activity and elevated reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS) are not merely bystander phenomena; they are central drivers of disease progression, severity, and broader metabolic complications. The evidence from the three branch reports converges on a single picture: oxidative stress worsens steatosis, promotes inflammation, drives fibrosis and cirrhosis, and extends beyond the liver to cardiovascular and metabolic disease [N2-F2][N3-R1][N5-F3][N2-R5]. The core mechanism is a failure of the liver’s antioxidant defense system. Nrf2 is the master regulator of antioxidant enzymes, including SOD, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, glutathione S-transferases, glutathione reductase, and other protective proteins involved in detoxification and elimination of oxidative stress [N1-F1][N1-R2]. When this system is impaired, ROS/RNS production exceeds clearance, leading to oxidative/nitrosative stress. The MASLD review explicitly states that oxidative/nitrosative stress is caused by imbalance between ROS/RNS and antioxidant defenses, and that this imbalance leads to cellular lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endoplasmic reticulum stress [N5-F3]. It also notes that antioxidant enzyme expression/activity changes during MASLD development and progression, with decreased antioxidant capacity in advanced disease [N5-F3].

This means that impaired antioxidant enzyme activity does not simply reduce ROS clearance; it shifts the liver into a pro-oxidant state in which ROS/RNS accumulate, oxidize lipids and proteins, and damage mitochondrial function. The same review states that oxidative stress is closely linked to cardiovascular complications such as atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure, highlighting a broader metabolic burden [N2-R5]. The MASLD review further links oxidative stress to lipid metabolism dysregulation, insulin resistance, and mitochondrial dysfunction, emphasizing that oxidative stress is a starting point of hepatic damage and important in MASLD progression [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In other words, reduced antioxidant capacity worsens the redox environment, which in turn worsens lipid accumulation and insulin resistance, creating a self-reinforcing cycle [N2-F2][N5-F3].

Oxidative stress is a central driver of MASLD progression and severity. The MASLD review describes MASLD as a spectrum from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, with mitochondrial dysfunction impairing lipid metabolism and increasing oxidative stress [N2-F2]. The oxidative stress in liver disease review states that oxidative stress plays a crucial role in liver disease progression to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) [N3-R1]. This supports the idea that oxidative stress is not only a downstream feature of MASLD but an active contributor to disease severity.

At the histopathological level, oxidative stress promotes inflammation and fibrosis. The oxidative stress in liver disease review explicitly states that oxidative stress regulates inflammatory pathways [N3-R2], while the MASLD review notes that oxidative/nitrosative stress leads to cellular lipotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endoplasmic reticulum stress [N5-F3]. This aligns with the broader pathophysiology of MASLD: oxidative stress injures hepatocytes, recruits inflammatory cells, and activates fibrogenic responses [N2-F2][N3-R1][N5-F3]. The review also notes that in advanced MASLD, antioxidant enzyme expression/activity generally decreases, further exacerbating damage [N5-F3]. That is, ROS/RNS elevation in the early stages may be compensated by upregulated antioxidant defenses, but in later stages, the system fails and disease worsens.

Evidence for cirrhosis or advanced fibrosis linked to ROS/RNS elevation is strong. The MASLD review states that MASLD encompasses a spectrum from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis [N2-F2]. The oxidative stress in liver disease review states that oxidative stress plays a crucial role in liver disease progression to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC [N3-R1]. The MASLD review also notes that oxidative stress is closely linked to cardiovascular complications, including atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure [N2-R5]. Taken together, these sources indicate that ROS/RNS elevation is associated with advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis, as well as with systemic metabolic complications [N3-R1][N2-R5].

### 3) Beyond the liver: cardiovascular and metabolic consequences

The evidence goes well beyond the liver. Oxidative stress in MASLD is closely linked to cardiovascular complications such as atherosclerosis, hypertension, and heart failure [N2-R5]. The MASLD review also states that oxidative stress and mitochondrial antioxidant defense depletion play an important role in disease progression in MAFLD/NASH [N3-R5]. This means that impaired antioxidant activity and elevated ROS/RNS are not confined to hepatic injury; they contribute to broader metabolic dysfunction and cardiovascular disease [N2-R5][N3-R5].

These effects are likely amplified by lipid metabolism and insulin resistance. The MASLD review states that MASLD is closely related to metabolic syndrome, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia [N2-F2]. It also notes that oxidative stress is the starting point of hepatic damage and is important in MASLD progression [N5-F3]. This implies that lipid accumulation and insulin resistance increase ROS/RNS production and reduce antioxidant capacity, creating a feedback loop that worsens redox imbalance [N2-F2][N5-F3]. In turn, redox imbalance can impair lipid metabolism, further fueling steatosis and inflammation [N2-F2][N5-F3].

### 4) What the evidence says about biomarkers and translational limits

The evidence base for oxidative stress in MASLD is substantial, but it is not yet definitive. The branch reports emphasize that biomarkers are important but not fully reliable. The oxidative stress in liver disease review states that oxidative stress not only contributes to NAFLD but also regulates inflammatory pathways [N3-R2], suggesting that biomarker elevation may reflect downstream or indirect changes rather than a direct readout of oxidative stress. In practical terms, the clinical consequences of impaired antioxidant activity and elevated ROS/RNS in MASLD are multiple and interconnected. Second, it is associated with advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis [N3-R1][N2-R5]. Third, it extends beyond the liver to cardiovascular and metabolic complications [N2-R5][N3-R5]. In patients with MASLD, impaired antioxidant enzyme activity and elevated ROS/RNS levels are major contributors to disease progression and severity. The main antioxidant defenses involved are Nrf2-regulated antioxidant enzymes, SOD, catalase, and glutathione-related pathways, which work together to clear ROS/RNS [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R5].
